reception.text: An Associated Press dispatch reported that steps were taken to carry out the proclamation as soon as it was received, and described the half-staff orders that followed.
reception.source: Los Angeles Herald, June 25, 1908, "Government to Honor Memory"

reception.text: California papers printed the text or a summary, including the San Luis Obispo Tribune under the headline "ROOSEVELT GIVES HIGH PRAISE TO CLEVELAND."
reception.source: Fresno Bee, June 24; Riverside Enterprise, June 25; San Luis Obispo Tribune, June 30, 1908

reception.text: No editorial objection to the proclamation was found in California papers for June 24–30, 1908.

political_impact.text: Army posts, fleets, ships and naval stations were ordered to fly their colors at half staff for thirty days, and diplomatic and consular offices were to do the same.
The State Department told its overseas posts by telegraph instead of by mail, so the observance would be uniform in time, which the press called an innovation.
In San Francisco, the fleet in the harbor and the Presidio and bay forts fired half-hourly guns on the day of the funeral.
At Cleveland's wish the funeral was private, with no eulogy; Mrs. Cleveland declined a military funeral, and Roosevelt attended the simple service at Westland.

legacy.text: The proclamation had no legal effect and carries no legacy of its own beyond the mourning it marked; what stands out is the warmth of its tribute to a man of the other party.

related.note: Roosevelt's proclamation on the death of William McKinley, which follows a different form.
